title: JSON padding & annotation fuzz suite for schema conformance
body:
Purpose:
This is a working prompt-suite designed to stress JSON schema adherence for onboarding models that must produce structured outputs. Unlike other prompt sets focused on semantic variations, this file targets formatting, annotations, and odd-but-valid/invalid JSON patterns that commonly break downstream parsers and type-checkers.

Quick notes (notes-to-self style):
- Goal: push models to emit JSON with surprising whitespace, annotations, unicode, and padding so we can classify failure modes.
- Not intended as final canonical prompts; many prompts are terse / intentionally ambiguous to reveal brittle model heuristics.
- We'll run these through the eval harness (see linked_artifacts) and collect parse-fail vs schema-violation stats.

Top-level target schema (for reference in tests):
- object: {
    id: string (uuid v4),
    created_at: string (ISO8601),
    user: { name: string, email: string|null },
    items: array of objects [{ sku: string, qty: integer >=1, price: number }],
    metadata: object (arbitrary key:value strings)
  }
(We supply this as human text so eval harness can load the JSON Schema file at repo path.)

Prompt categories and example seeds:
1) Padding / whitespace variants
- Seed: "Return the order object as JSON. Insert extra spaces, newlines, and tabs randomly inside and between tokens."
- Tests: leading/trailing spaces, lines with only spaces, tabs between keys and colons, multiple blank lines, CRLF vs LF, mixed indentation.
- Failure cases we expect: model injects human commentary lines ("note:"), or splits string values across lines without proper escaping.

2) Annotation and inline commentary
- Seed: "Emit only JSON. Some fields may have inline parenthetical comments — if you include a comment, mark it as a string field called '_comment' next to the field."
- Variation: encourage use of C-style comments (/* */) or JSON-with-comments. Expect models sometimes output // or /* */ which breaks strict parsers.
- Targeted check: parser rejects comments unless we map them to _comment fields.

3) Character encodings, BOM, and unicode escapes
- Seed: "Produce JSON that includes names with accented characters, ZWNBSP, zero-width joiners, emoji, and explicit \uXXXX escape sequences."
- Tests: BOM at start (\uFEFF), unescaped control chars (\u0007), surrogate pairs, and mixed use of \u vs literal characters.
- Failure modes: JSON parsing errors, schema validators treating strings differently due to normalization.

4) Trailing commas / single-quoted strings / unquoted keys
- Seed: "Return the object but feel free to use relaxed JS-style object syntax (single quotes, trailing commas, unquoted keys)."
- Goal: see if models prefer JS-like shorthand and whether post-processing can reliably canonicalize.

5) Duplicate keys and key ordering stress
- Seed: "Include two 'items' entries; put a short summary field earlier and the full 'items' later."
- Cases: duplicate keys with different values, keys appearing in different orders, ordering-sensitive consumers.
- Evaluation: record which value wins after parser (e.g., last-wins in V8), compare to schema expectation.

6) Numeric edgecases and scientific notation
- Seed: "Emit prices using integers, floats, zero-padded numbers, scientific notation (1e3), and negative zero (-0)."
- Validate: schema numeric type acceptance, decimal precision, and whether string quoting occurs.

7) Arrays with heterogeneous element types
- Seed: "Put mixed-type elements in items array (string sku, null, object, number) intentionally to test type enforcement."
- Expectation: strict schema rejects; some models will coerce types to strings.

8) Escaped separators and nested JSON-as-string
- Seed: "One field (metadata.notes) should include a JSON blob encoded as a string. Use lots of escaped quotes and backslashes."
- Check: unescaping pipeline, double-encoded JSON, and accidental attempt by model to embed unescaped JSON.

9) Large payload and chunking behavior
- Seed: "Emit an items array with 200 entries. Add intermittent "// pagination" style comments between entries."
- Why: tests batching/stream outputs and streaming/continuation behaviors where model might break JSON across chunks.

10) Schema-guided hints vs adversarial instructions
- Seed A (helpful): "Follow the schema exactly: include id (uuid v4), created_at ISO8601, user.name, user.email, items list..."
- Seed B (adversarial): "You can be creative with structure; add extra helpful fields and human explanations inline."
- Compare: see how strongly model follows schema when explicitly prompted vs when given freedom.

Evaluation plan and labels:
- Parseable: boolean (model output parsed by strict JSON parser).
- Conforms_schema: boolean (AJV/JSON Schema validation passes).
- Soft_conform: list of minor issues (e.g., types coerced to strings, missing optional fields).
- Fail_reasons: list of categories: UNESCAPED_CONTROL_CHARS, TRAILING_COMMA, COMMENTS_PRESENT, DUPLICATE_KEYS, WRONG_TYPES, NON_JSON_SYNTAX, TRUNCATED_STREAM, BOM_PRESENT.
- Severity: minor|major|blocking.

Test harness notes (how to run):
- Use eval harness job: run tests against model_version candidate with flags --strict-json (fail on any parse error) and --lenient-json (attempt automatic canonicalization).
- Collect both raw output and canonicalized output; canonicalizer applies: remove comments if present, strip BOM, convert single quotes to double quotes (only when safe), remove trailing commas, and canonicalize numeric strings if possible.
- Store raw outputs in s3://redwood-evals/raw/json-padding-suite/ and canonicalized outputs in s3://redwood-evals/processed/json-padding-suite/.

Metrics we will capture per prompt:
- parse_rate (fraction parseable),
- schema_pass_rate (fraction that pass AJV),
- average_repair_distance (Levenshtein between raw and canonicalized),
- common_failure_modes (top 5),
- time_to_first_token and token_count to eyeball cost impact of extra annotations.

Immediate tasks / TODOs:
- [ ] Convert these seed prompts into the eval YAML format (Marta).
- [ ] Add precise regexes for UUID/ISO in the harness (Jonah).
- [ ] Add a canonicalizer PR that is conservative and logs transformations (Liam).
- [ ] Run on two model families: baseline-1 (open), baseline-2 (quantized) and collect results.

Open questions / discussion points:
- How aggressive should canonicalizer be? If it changes semantics (e.g., coerce numeric string to number) we may mask model errors.
- For duplicate keys, do we mark parseable but ambiguous, or mark as schema fail? (proposal: mark ambiguous + severity major).
- How to flag streaming truncation vs model simply producing smaller arrays? Need heuristics: expect length N, check for trailing commas or incomplete braces.

Example prompt variants (short list to paste into harness):
- "Emit only the order JSON. No commentary. Keep keys exactly as in the schema. Randomly add a BOM at the start or a trailing newline."
- "Return the order but please include inline comments like // this price is estimate. If you include a comment, also add a '_comment' sibling string field."
- "Print the order but use single-quoted strings and trailing commas. Do not explain."
- "Produce the order and intentionally add duplicate 'items' key with differing arrays. Put a short 'summary' before and 'items' full later."

Appendix: quick failure taxonomy (copyable):
- UNESCAPED_CTRL: model emitted U+0000..U+001F in strings unescaped.
- COMMENT_SYNTAX: model emitted // or /* */ comments.
- TRAILING_COMMA: arrays/objects end with comma.
- SINGLE_QUOTES: single-quoted strings used.
- UNQUOTED_KEYS: keys not wrapped in double quotes.
- DUP_KEYS: duplicate object keys with differing values.
- TRUNCATED: output ends before closing braces.
- BOM: leading U+FEFF present.

Last words: This is intentionally messy; the goal is to capture brittle behaviors early in onboarding so we can either tune prompts or add conservative post-processing. Keep prompts short and adversarial in many runs — we want a distribution of failure types, not a pass-only set.
